$comment: What text a resource's bytes are, as every reader of one must read them: the cases of the rule docs/protocol/W3C-SELECTORS.md states of a resource's text, which is the MIME Sniffing Standard's reading of a content type and the Encoding Standard's reading of the bytes, as a browser follows the two. An offset counts the code points of this text (offset-cases.json), so two readers that make different texts of the same bytes put one annotation in two places. THE RULE, IN SHORT; the document has it whole. (1) The charset is the content type's `charset` parameter as the MIME Sniffing Standard parses a MIME type: the name whole and in any case, the first of several, a quoted value's content. A parameter with no value is no parameter, and a content type that is no MIME type has none. No charset, or an empty one, is UTF-8. (2) The charset is a label of the Encoding Standard, in any case and with ASCII white space around it dropped. Anything else is refused, and so is a label of the standard's `replacement` encoding: the refusal names the label, and is made whatever the bytes are. (3) Bytes that begin with the byte-order mark of UTF-8 (EF BB BF), of UTF-16BE (FE FF) or of UTF-16LE (FF FE) are in that encoding, whatever charset was stated, and the mark is not part of the text. A mark anywhere else is U+FEFF, a character like any other. (4) The bytes are decoded by the standard's decoder for the encoding: what the encoding does not have is U+FFFD, as many as that decoder emits and no more. (5) A refusal is the reader's own failure, of the kind its other failures are. (6) Only a media type whose bytes are its text is read. The media type is the content type without its parameters, in lower case. One the media-type registry lists (specs/src/media-types/registry.json) is read where its `textSource` there is `decode`, and one the registry does not list is read where it is a `text/` type. Any other is refused, before its charset is read and whatever its bytes are: a type whose text is derived from its bytes (a PDF), and a type with no text (an image). The refusal names the media type. A CASE is the `contentType` the bytes came with, the `bytes` in hexadecimal, two digits to a byte and a space between bytes, and either the `text` they are or `refused`, what the refusal names: the label of a charset that is refused, or a media type whose bytes are not its text. In this file a control character, U+FEFF, U+FFFD and a private-use character are written as escapes, so that each can be seen. THE OTHER TABLE. encoding-cases.json, beside this one, is generated: it holds every label of the standard and every byte of each of its single-byte encodings. This one holds what is said of a content type, of a label, of a mark, of malformed UTF-8 and UTF-16, and of a media type whose text is not its bytes. NOT HELD. What a reader makes of bytes in the standard's seven legacy multi-byte encodings (Big5, EUC-JP, EUC-KR, gb18030, GBK, ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS): each reader reads those with a decoder of its own. A reader may decode fewer encodings than the standard has, and refuses what it does not decode by name: an SDK may be built to decode UTF-8 alone. HOW IT IS RUN. Every SDK runs every case through what its client reads a resource's content with, by which a worker reads the text it counts offsets in: it keeps (6), and then reads by (1) to (5). A reader of UTF-8 alone reads each case as it is here or refuses it. A reader in another language runs them too. Add a case here before changing a reader.
